paragraphs.heading: Describing a quantum state
paragraphs.text: In quantum mechanics, a wave function is the mathematical description of the quantum state of an isolated system. It is usually written with the Greek letter psi, either ψ or Ψ. Wave functions take complex values. For example, a wave function might give a complex number to each point in some region of space.

paragraphs.heading: From numbers to chances
paragraphs.text: The Born rule turns these complex numbers, called probability amplitudes, into real probabilities. In one common form, the squared modulus of a wave function that depends on position is the probability density of finding a particle at a given place. The squared modulus, integrated over every degree of freedom of the system, must come to 1, a requirement called normalization. Its values are complex, so the only things you can measure are its relative magnitude and its relative phase. To predict measurements, you apply quantum operators, whose eigenvalues are the possible results, and work out the statistics.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is called a wave
paragraphs.text: The Schrödinger equation determines how wave functions change over time. Since that equation is mathematically a kind of wave equation, a wave function behaves much like a water wave or a wave on a string. This explains the name, and it gives rise to wave–particle duality. Still, whether the wave function describes something physical remains open to different interpretations, which sets it apart from ordinary mechanical waves.

paragraphs.heading: Adding and converting
paragraphs.text: Under the superposition principle, you can add wave functions and scale them by complex numbers to get new ones, forming a Hilbert space. Wave functions also need not depend on position; they can depend on momentum instead, and a Fourier transform converts one form into the other. Particles such as electrons and photons have nonzero spin, so their wave function includes spin as a separate, discrete variable. At each point in space it then gives one complex number for each possible spin value, often written as a column, for instance a 2 × 1 column vector when the particle is a non-relativistic electron with spin 1⁄2.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: In 1916 Max Planck linked a photon's momentum p and wavelength λ through λ = h/p. De Broglie, in 1923, was the first to propose that this relation also applies to particles that have mass. In 1926 Schrödinger published the wave equation now named after him, and its solutions are the wave functions of a quantum system. Yet no one was clear how to interpret it.

paragraphs.heading: A particle is not a smear
paragraphs.text: At first, Schrödinger and others thought a wave function showed a particle spread out, with most of it where the wave function is large. That idea failed for scattering. A wave packet that scatters off a target spreads out in every direction, but a scattered particle may go any way without breaking up and flying off in all directions at once.

paragraphs.heading: Born's answer
paragraphs.text: In 1926, Max Born offered a different view: the wave function is a probability amplitude. This ties the calculations of quantum mechanics directly to the odds seen in experiments. The view is part of the Copenhagen interpretation, though many other interpretations of quantum mechanics exist.
